name: Operating Systems
desc: Processes, threads, IPC, CPU scheduling, synchronization, deadlocks, memory management, virtual memory, file systems

topics.name: OS Basics, Types & Kernel
notes: An **OS** is an interface between hardware and application programs, a **collection of programs that manages hardware resources**, and a **service provider** to programs. Services are accessed through **system calls**.

**Bootstrap program**: the initial program run at power-up (stored in ROM/firmware). It initialises CPU registers, device controllers and memory, then loads the OS kernel. On multi-OS machines the **boot loader** decides which OS to load.

**Kernel**: core of the OS, always in memory, first part loaded at boot. Modern kernels **can load modules at run time**. Types: **monolithic** (Linux), **microkernel** (QNX, Mach), **hybrid** (Windows NT, **macOS/OS X**).
**Trap/exception** = a **software-generated interrupt** caused by an error (divide by zero, invalid memory access) or by a user request (system call).

**Real-time OS** examples: **RTLinux, VxWorks, QNX, Windows CE**. **Palm OS is NOT real-time**. Hard RTOS: a task **must** meet its deadline, has **less jitter**; interrupt latency must be **minimal**.

**Multiprogramming**: several processes in memory at once → **increases CPU utilisation** (CPU time is used productively). **Uniprogramming/uniprocessing**: one process at a time. **Multiprocessing**: several CPUs run processes truly in parallel.
**Network OS** runs on the **server**. A **distributed OS** makes many machines look like one system.
**Transient OS code** comes and goes as needed, so it **changes** the size of the OS in memory. The OS sits in **low or high memory, depending on the location of the interrupt vector**.
The **command interpreter (shell)** gets and executes the next user-specified command. If a process fails, the OS writes the error information to a **log file**.

topics.name: Processes, PCB & Process States
notes: **Process** = program in execution. Memory layout: **text (code), data (globals), heap (dynamic), stack** (function parameters, local variables, return addresses).
**States**: New → Ready → Running → Waiting (Blocked) → Ready … → Terminated. There is no "Old" state.
Time slice expires → **Running → Ready**. I/O completes → **Waiting → Ready**. I/O request → Running → Waiting. The only transition the process itself starts is **block** (by requesting I/O).

**PCB** (process control block) = **data structure** holding: process state, PC, CPU registers, scheduling info, memory-management info, accounting and I/O status. All PCBs are kept in the **process table**.
Each process has its own **address space, global variables, open files, pending alarms, signals and signal handlers**. Threads of a process share these.
**Queues**: job queue (all processes), **ready queue** (in memory, waiting for CPU), device/I/O queues. There is no "PCB queue".

**Schedulers**: **long-term** (job scheduler, chooses which processes enter the ready queue — controls the **degree of multiprogramming**); **short-term** (CPU scheduler, picks the next process to run — runs very often); **medium-term** (swapping out/in). Main difference between short- and long-term: **frequency of execution**.
**Dispatcher** gives the CPU to the process chosen by the short-term scheduler (context switch, switch to user mode, jump). **Dispatch latency** = time to stop one process and start another.
**Context switch** (also called process switch or task switch): save the old PCB, load the new one. The **TLB** need not be saved. The PCB does not contain "context switch time".

**fork()** returns **0 to the child** and the **child's PID (> 0) to the parent**. **wait()** makes the parent wait for a child to terminate. **exec()** loads a new program into the process. Child finishes but parent hasn't called wait → **zombie**. Parent dies first → **orphan**.
**Cascading termination**: when a parent terminates (normally or abnormally), all its children are terminated too.

topics.name: Threads & Multithreading
notes: **Thread** = basic unit of CPU utilisation: its own **thread ID, PC, register set and stack**; shares code, data, open files and signals with other threads of the process.
Benefits of multithreading: **responsiveness, resource sharing, economy** (cheaper to create/switch than processes), **scalability** on multicore.

**User-level threads**: managed by a thread library, **the kernel does not know them, so the kernel cannot schedule them**; fast switching, but one blocking call can block the whole process (many-to-one).
**Kernel-level threads**: managed and **scheduled by the kernel**; slower to create but can run in parallel.
Models: **Many-to-one** (many user threads → 1 kernel thread; no parallelism), **One-to-one** (Linux, Windows; more overhead), **Many-to-many** (flexible).
A **single thread of control** lets a process do **only one task at a time**.
**Multithreaded programs are more prone to deadlocks** (more locks, more interleavings).
Thread libraries: **POSIX Pthreads**, Windows threads, Java threads.

topics.name: Inter-Process Communication
notes: **IPC** allows processes to **communicate and synchronise their actions**. Two models: **shared memory** and **message passing**. A process that can be affected by others is **cooperating**.

**Message passing** lets processes communicate **without sharing the same address space**. Operations: **send** and **receive**. Messages can be **fixed or variable size**. The connection is called a **communication link**.

**Direct communication**: name the other process explicitly; **a link is associated with exactly two processes**, and exactly one link exists per pair. **Indirect communication**: messages go through a **mailbox (port)**.
**Blocking (synchronous) send**: the sender waits until the message is received. **Non-blocking (asynchronous) send**: the sender sends and **resumes operation**.
Buffering: **Zero capacity** = **no buffering**; sender **blocks until the receiver receives** (rendezvous). **Bounded and unbounded capacity** = **automatic buffering**.
**RPC (Remote Procedure Call)**: IPC between processes on **different systems** using message-based communication.
Other IPC: **pipes** (ordinary/unnamed between related processes, named pipes/FIFOs), **sockets**, signals, message queues.

topics.name: CPU Scheduling Concepts & Criteria
notes: **CPU scheduling is the basis of multiprogrammed operating systems**; it aims to **increase CPU utilisation and throughput** and **decrease turnaround, waiting and response time**.
Process execution alternates **CPU bursts and I/O bursts**. **I/O-bound** program → **many short CPU bursts**; CPU-bound → a few long CPU bursts.

**Turnaround time** = completion − arrival (submission). **Waiting time** = total time in the **ready queue** = turnaround − burst. **Response time** = time from submission to the **first response**. **Throughput** = processes completed per unit time.
**Non-preemptive** scheduling happens only when a process switches **running → waiting** or **terminates**. **Preemptive** also happens on running → ready (timer) and waiting → ready.
**Preemptive scheduling** = making logically runnable processes temporarily suspended. It may cause **starvation** (as can SRTF and priority).
**Starvation (indefinite blocking)** of low-priority processes is solved by **aging** (gradually raising the priority of waiting processes).
**Priority inversion**: a high-priority task is indirectly preempted by a medium-priority task (because a low-priority task holds its lock). Fix: **priority inheritance**.

**Multilevel queue**: processes are classified into groups (foreground/background), each with its own queue; classification is permanent. **Multilevel feedback queue**: processes **can move between queues**.
**Round robin** is preemptive and uses a **time quantum**: a very large quantum → behaves like **FCFS**; a very small quantum → too many context switches.

topics.name: Scheduling Numericals (FCFS, SJF, SRTF, RR, Priority)
notes: **Gantt chart first**, then: Turnaround = Completion − Arrival; Waiting = Turnaround − Burst; Response = First run − Arrival.
FCFS P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 (all at 0): waits 0, 24, 27 → **avg 17**. Order P2, P3, P1 → avg **3** (convoy effect).
**SJF is optimal** — minimum average waiting time (among non-preemptive). **SRTF** is its preemptive version.

topics.name: Concurrency, Critical Section & Semaphores
notes: **Race condition**: several processes access shared data concurrently and the result depends on the order of access.

**Critical-section solution requirements**: (1) **Mutual exclusion** — if one process is in its CS, no other is in theirs; (2) **Progress** — if no one is in the CS, the choice of who enters next can't be postponed indefinitely; (3) **Bounded waiting** — there's a limit on how many times others can enter **after a process has requested entry and before that request is granted**.
**Peterson's solution** (2 processes) uses **2 shared variables**: `flag[2]` and `turn`. Minimum shared variables for the CS problem = 2.

**Semaphore** = integer variable accessed only through two **atomic** operations: **wait (P, down)** and **signal (V, up)**. Binary semaphore (0/1) ≈ **mutex lock**. Counting semaphore for multiple instances. Classical semaphore value **cannot drop below zero**.
Counting semaphore arithmetic: final = initial − (number of P) + (number of V). e.g. 10 − 6 + 4 = 8.
Misuse: `signal(mutex) … CS … wait(mutex)` → **several processes in the CS** (no mutual exclusion). `wait(mutex) … CS … wait(mutex)` → **deadlock**.

**Monitor**: high-level construct that encapsulates **shared data, the procedures on it, and synchronisation** — only one process is active inside at a time. Waiting inside uses **condition variables** (`condition x; x.wait(); x.signal();`).
Synchronisation can be done in **hardware** (test-and-set, compare-and-swap, disabling interrupts) and **software** (Peterson, semaphores, monitors).
Classic problems: **producer–consumer (bounded buffer)**, **readers–writers**, **dining philosophers**.

topics.name: Deadlocks
notes: **Deadlock**: a set of processes where **each is blocked forever**, waiting for a resource held by another in the set.
**Four necessary conditions** (all must hold): **Mutual exclusion** (≥ 1 non-sharable resource), **Hold and wait** (hold ≥ 1 resource and wait for more), **No preemption**, **Circular wait**.

**Prevention** = make sure **at least one** condition cannot hold. Circular wait → **impose a linear ordering of resource types**. Hold & wait → request everything at once (**low resource utilisation**, possible starvation). No preemption → if a request can't be granted, **preempt all resources currently held**. Mutual exclusion is not required for sharable resources.

**Avoidance** needs a-priori info on the **maximum** need of each process. It dynamically examines the **resource-allocation state**. **Safe state** ⇔ there is a **safe sequence**. Unsafe ≠ deadlock (but may lead to it).

**Banker's algorithm**: Need = Max − Allocation. Find a process whose Need ≤ Available, let it finish, add its Allocation back to Available, repeat. It handles **multiple instances** but is **less efficient** than the resource-allocation-graph algorithm.

**Resource-allocation graph** (and **wait-for graph**) avoidance/detection works only for **single-instance** resources. In a wait-for graph, edge **Pi → Pj means Pi waits for Pj** to release a resource; **a cycle means deadlock** (single instance).
Detection frequency: if deadlocks occur **frequently**, run detection **frequently**. Recovery: abort processes or preempt resources.
**Minimum resources to guarantee no deadlock**: n processes each needing up to k units → **n(k − 1) + 1**.
Requests and releases of resources are **system calls**. A **reusable resource** can be used by one process at a time and is not depleted by use.

topics.name: Memory Management: Allocation, Paging & Segmentation
notes: **Logical (virtual) address** generated by the CPU; **physical address** seen by memory. **MMU** maps them. Protection: every CPU address is checked against the **relocation (base) and limit registers**.
**Contiguous allocation**: First fit (first hole big enough), **Best fit** (smallest adequate hole), **Worst fit** (largest hole). First and best fit are generally better than worst fit.

**External fragmentation**: enough total free memory, but not contiguous → fix with **compaction** or paging. **Internal fragmentation**: unused space inside an allocated block (paging has it in the last page).

**Paging**: logical memory → fixed-size **pages**; physical → **frames** of the same size. No external fragmentation. Address = page number + offset. The OS keeps a **frame table** (which frames are free/allocated).
Page table size = number of pages × entry size. 32-bit address, 4 KB pages → 2²⁰ pages; with 4-byte entries → 4 MB page table.
**Segmentation**: variable-size logical units (code, stack, data); address = (segment, offset); has external fragmentation.
**Dynamic loading**: routines are loaded only when called; **user programs can implement it without special OS/hardware support**. **Dynamic linking** needs OS support.
**Swapping**: move a process out to disk and back. **Never swap a process with pending I/O** into its own memory (or do I/O only into OS buffers).
**Device drivers** present a uniform device-access interface to the I/O subsystem.

topics.name: Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
notes: **Demand paging**: load a page only when it is referenced. A missing page → **page fault** → OS loads it from disk.
**Effective access time** = (1 − p) × memory access + p × page-fault service time. Even p = 0.001 slows memory a lot (200 ns → ~8.2 µs with 8 ms faults).

Page replacement: **FIFO** (oldest page out; suffers **Belady's anomaly** — more frames can mean MORE faults), **Optimal/OPT** (replace the page not used for the longest time in future — lowest faults, not implementable), **LRU** (least recently used — good approximation; stack algorithm, no Belady's anomaly).
Classic string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 1 2 0 1 7 0 1 with 3 frames → **FIFO 15, LRU 12, OPT 9** faults.
Belady string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 → FIFO **9 faults with 3 frames, 10 with 4 frames**.
**Thrashing**: a process spends more time paging than executing (too few frames). Fix: working-set model, page-fault-frequency control, lower the degree of multiprogramming.
**Working set** = pages referenced in the last Δ references. If the sum of working sets exceeds the available frames, **the OS suspends (swaps out) a process**.
**Copy-on-write**: after fork, parent and child share pages until one writes.

topics.name: File Systems & Disk Scheduling
notes: Information about all files is kept in a **directory structure** (on disk). The OS keeps an in-memory **open-file table**. File metadata is kept in a **file control block (FCB)** / inode.

Directory structures: **single-level** (all files in the same directory — name clashes), **two-level** (one per user), **tree-structured**, **acyclic graph** (shared files via links; the OS **ignores links when traversing** to keep the structure acyclic), general graph.

**Allocation methods**: **Contiguous** (fast, supports direct access, external fragmentation), **Linked** (no external fragmentation, slow random access; FAT is a variant), **Indexed** (index block holds pointers; supports direct access; Unix inodes).
Access methods: **sequential**, **direct (random)**, indexed.
Free-space management: **bit vector**, linked list, grouping, counting.

**Disk scheduling**: FCFS, **SSTF** (shortest seek first — may starve), **SCAN** (elevator), **C-SCAN**, LOOK, C-LOOK. Example queue 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 with the head at 53 → **FCFS 640**, **SSTF 236** cylinders.
Disk access time = **seek time + rotational latency + transfer time**.

questions.q: What is an operating system?
o: interface between the hardware and application programs
collection of programs that manages hardware resources
system service provider to the application programs
w: An OS is all three: interface, resource manager and service provider.

questions.q: Which one of the following is not a real time operating system?
w: Palm OS was a PDA operating system, not a real-time one.
questions.h: RTOS family: RTLinux, VxWorks, QNX, Windows CE — not Palm OS.

questions.q: Which one of the following is a real time operating system?
w: It is real-time, but so are the others.
It is real-time, but so are the others.
It is real-time, but so are the others.
Windows CE, RTLinux and VxWorks are all real-time OSs.
questions.h: Windows CE, RTLinux, VxWorks → all RTOS.

questions.q: In real time operating system ____________
o: process scheduling can be done only once
all processes have the same priority
a task must be serviced by its deadline period

questions.q: Hard real time operating system has ______________ jitter than a soft real time operating system.
w: Hard real-time needs very predictable timing → less jitter.
questions.h: Hard RT = strict timing = less jitter.

questions.q: For real time operating systems, interrupt latency should be ____________
w: Fast, bounded response to events is essential.

questions.q: A missed deadline in a HARD real-time system means:
o: A system failure — results after the deadline are useless or dangerous
Nothing, the task just runs later
The task gets higher priority next time
questions.h: Hard RT miss = failure; soft RT miss = degraded quality.

questions.q: What does OS X has?
w: OS X's XNU is not a pure microkernel.
XNU combines the Mach microkernel with BSD components.

questions.q: Linux uses which kernel architecture?
w: All core services run in kernel space; modules can be loaded at run time.

questions.q: In a microkernel architecture:
o: All services run in kernel mode
Only minimal services (IPC, basic scheduling, memory) run in the kernel; others run in user space
Device drivers must be in the kernel
questions.h: Microkernel = tiny kernel, services in user space.

questions.q: Which one of the following is not true?
o: kernel remains in the memory during the entire computer session
kernel is made of various modules which can not be loaded in running operating system
kernel is the first part of the operating system to load into memory during booting
kernel is the program that constitutes the central core of the operating system
w: False — modern kernels load modules dynamically (e.g. Linux insmod/modprobe).
questions.h: Modules CAN be loaded into a running kernel.

questions.q: The initial program that is run when the computer is powered up is called __________
w: The boot loader chooses/loads an OS; the first program is the bootstrap.
Stored in ROM/firmware; it starts everything.

questions.q: The _______ program initializes all aspects of the system, from CPU registers to device controllers and the contents of main memory, and then starts the operating system.
w: It initialises the hardware and loads the kernel.
A C entry point, not boot.
Related, but the bank (and Galvin) uses "bootstrap" here.
ROM is where the bootstrap is stored.

questions.q: On systems where there are multiple operating system, the decision to load a particular one is done by _____________
w: e.g. GRUB lets you choose which OS to boot.
Bootstrap starts the machine; the boot loader picks the OS.

questions.q: The bootstrap program is usually stored in:
w: The CPU can't read the disk without code first.

questions.q: What is a trap/exception?
o: hardware generated interrupt caused by an error
software generated interrupt caused by an error
user generated interrupt caused by an error
w: e.g. divide-by-zero, invalid memory access, or a system call.

questions.q: A system call made by a user program switches the CPU from:
o: User mode to kernel mode (through a trap)
w: The OS then runs the requested service.
questions.h: System call = trap into kernel mode.

questions.q: To access the services of the operating system, the interface is provided by the ___________
w: System calls are the interface between a program and the OS.
An API usually calls system calls underneath.

questions.q: What is the main function of the command interpreter?
o: to provide the interface between the API and application program
to handle the files in the operating system
to get and execute the next user-specified command
w: The shell reads a command and runs it.

questions.q: Where is the operating system placed in the memory?
o: either low or high memory (depending on the location of interrupt vector)
w: The OS is usually placed where the interrupt vector is.
Only if the interrupt vector is in low memory.
Only if the interrupt vector is in high memory.
questions.h: OS goes with the interrupt vector.

questions.q: The main memory accommodates ____________
w: The CPU isn't stored in memory.
True, but the bank wants the OS.
Main memory must hold the operating system (and also user processes).
The CPU is not in memory.
questions.h: Memory holds the OS (+ user processes).
questions.f: Galvin: "main memory must accommodate both the operating system and the various user processes". The bank key is "operating system".

questions.q: Transient operating system code is a code that ____________
w: Loaded only when needed, freed afterwards.

questions.q: Using transient code, _______ the size of the operating system during program execution.
w: Code is loaded and unloaded, so the OS footprint changes.

questions.q: Network operating system runs on ___________
o: both server and every system in the network
w: A NOS runs on the server and provides network services.

questions.q: What are the types of distributed operating systems?
w: Network OSs are one type of distributed system.
The other two are made up.

questions.q: The systems which allow only one process execution at a time, are called __________
w: Also used informally, but the bank key is uniprocessing.
Only one process runs at a time.
questions.f: Many textbooks call this "uniprogramming". The bank key is "uniprocessing systems".

questions.q: With _____________ only one process can execute at a time; meanwhile all other process are waiting for the processor. With ______________ more than one process can be running simultaneously each on a different processor.
w: Multiprogramming keeps several processes in memory.
One process at a time vs. many CPUs running at once.

questions.q: In a multiprogramming environment __________
o: the processor executes more than one process at a time
the programs are developed by more than one person
more than one process resides in the memory
a single user can execute many programs at the same time
w: One CPU runs one process at any instant.
The CPU switches among them when one waits.

questions.q: What is the objective of multiprogramming?
o: Have a process running at all time
Have multiple programs waiting in a queue ready to run
w: A consequence, not the stated objective.
Keep the CPU busy while others wait for I/O.

questions.q: With multiprogramming ______ is used productively.
w: CPU time is not wasted waiting for I/O.

questions.q: Time-sharing (multitasking) systems are an extension of multiprogramming in which:
o: The CPU switches so frequently that each user can interact with their program
Only one job runs at a time
Jobs are run in batches with no interaction
w: Uses time slices for quick response.
questions.h: Time-sharing = multiprogramming + fast switching for interaction.

questions.q: Which one of the following errors will be handle by the operating system?
w: Handled, but so are the others.
Handled, but so are the others.
Handled, but so are the others.
The OS detects and handles hardware, I/O and network errors.

questions.q: If a process fails, most operating system write the error information to a ______
The operating system is responsible for?
w: Disk management covers formatting, booting and bad blocks.
questions.h: OS disk management = all of these.

questions.q: Which of the following is not the state of a process?
The state of a process is defined by __________
o: the current activity of the process
the final activity of the process
the activity just executed by the process
the activity to next be executed by the process
w: The state (new/ready/running/…) reflects what it is doing now.

questions.q: What is the ready state of a process?
o: when process is scheduled to run after some execution
when process is unable to run until some task has been completed
when process is using the CPU
w: It is ready and waiting for the CPU.
The first option is the bank answer.

questions.q: In a timeshare operating system, when the time slot assigned to a process is completed, the process switches from the current state to?
w: Preempted by the timer → back to the ready queue.

questions.q: Suppose that a process is in “Blocked” state waiting for some I/O service. When the service is completed, it goes to the __________
w: I/O done → ready queue → waits for the CPU.
questions.h: Waiting → (I/O done) → Ready, never straight to Running.

questions.q: A running process issues an I/O request. Its state changes to:
w: It can't continue until the I/O is done.
It waits for the I/O to complete.

questions.q: The only state transition that is initiated by the user process itself is __________
w: The process blocks itself by requesting I/O or an event.
questions.h: Process blocks itself; the OS does dispatch and wakeup.

questions.q: A process stack does not contain __________
w: PIDs are kept by the OS (in PCBs), not on the process stack.

questions.q: Dynamically allocated memory (malloc/new) of a process lives in the:
w: Grows and shrinks at run time.

questions.q: What is a Process Control Block?
w: The kernel data structure that represents a process.

questions.q: A Process Control Block(PCB) does not contain which of the following?
w: The bootstrap is firmware — nothing to do with a process.

questions.q: The context of a process in the PCB of a process does not contain __________
o: the value of the CPU registers
questions.h: PCB: state, PC, registers, memory info, I/O, accounting.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stored in a PCB?
o: The compiler used to build the program
questions.h: PCB = everything needed to resume the process.

questions.q: The entry of all the PCBs of the current processes is in __________
w: The kernel's table of all PCBs.

questions.q: The address of the next instruction to be executed by the current process is provided by the __________
w: PC holds the next instruction address.

questions.q: In operating system, each process has its own __________
o: pending alarms, signals and signal handlers
questions.h: Per process: address space, globals, files, signals.

questions.q: Which of the following is shared by threads of the same process but NOT between different processes?
questions.h: Threads share the process; they own PC, registers and stack.

questions.q: Which of the following do not belong to queues for processes?
The processes that are residing in main memory and are ready and waiting to execute are kept on a list called _____________
w: Holds all processes in the system.
In memory, waiting for the CPU.

questions.q: When the process issues an I/O request __________
o: It is placed in an I/O queue
It is placed in a waiting queue
It is placed in the ready queue
It is placed in the Job queue
w: It waits in the device's queue.
The standard term is I/O (device) queue.

questions.q: What will happen when a process terminates?
o: It is removed from all queues
It is removed from all, but the job queue
Its process control block is de-allocated
Its process control block is never de-allocated
w: The bank's answer: it leaves every queue.
Also happens eventually, but not the bank key.

questions.q: What is a long-term scheduler?
o: It selects processes which have to be brought into the ready queue
It selects processes which have to be executed next and allocates CPU
It selects processes which have to remove from memory by swapping

questions.q: What is a medium-term scheduler?
o: It selects which process has to be brought into the ready queue
It selects which process has to be executed next and allocates CPU
It selects which process to remove from memory by swapping
w: Swaps processes out and back in.

questions.q: What is a short-term scheduler?
o: It selects which process has to be brought into the ready queue
It selects which process has to be executed next and allocates CPU
It selects which process to remove from memory by swapping

questions.q: A process is selected from the ______ queue by the ________ scheduler, to be executed.
o: a few very short I/O bursts
w: The CPU scheduler picks from the ready queue.

questions.q: The primary distinction between the short term scheduler and the long term scheduler is __________
o: The type of processes they schedule
w: Short-term runs every few ms; long-term runs rarely.

questions.q: The degree of multiprogramming is controlled by the:
w: It decides how many processes are admitted to memory.
Picks the next process to run.
Can reduce it, but long-term controls it.
questions.h: Long-term controls how many are in memory.

questions.q: What is the degree of multiprogramming?
o: the number of processes executed per unit time
the number of processes in the ready queue
the number of processes in the I/O queue
the number of processes in memory
w: How many processes are loaded at once.

questions.q: If all processes I/O bound, the ready queue will almost always be ______ and the Short term Scheduler will have a ______ to do.
w: Processes sit in I/O queues, so the ready queue is nearly empty.
Empty queue means little scheduling work.
questions.h: All I/O-bound → empty ready queue, idle scheduler.

questions.q: Which module gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler?
w: Context switches, switches to user mode and jumps to the right place.
The scheduler chooses; the dispatcher hands over the CPU.

questions.q: The portion of the process scheduler in an operating system that dispatches processes is concerned with ____________
o: assigning ready processes to waiting queue
assigning running processes to blocked queue

questions.q: What is Dispatch latency?
o: the speed of dispatching a process from running to the ready state
the time of dispatching a process from running to ready state and keeping the CPU idle
the time to stop one process and start running another one
questions.h: Dispatch latency = stop one, start another.

questions.q: The switching of the CPU from one process or thread to another is called ____________
questions.h: Context switch = process switch = task switch.

questions.q: Which of the following need not necessarily be saved on a context switch between processes?
w: The TLB is flushed or tagged, not saved — it can be rebuilt.
Registers and PC must be saved.

questions.q: Which of the following does not interrupt a running process?
w: The scheduler runs because of interrupts; it doesn't interrupt by itself.
questions.h: Interrupts come from devices, timers and failures — not the scheduler.

questions.q: In UNIX, the return value for the fork system call is _____ for the child process and _____ for the parent process.
w: Child gets 0; parent gets the child's PID (positive).
Each fork doubles the number of processes.
That is the number of CHILD processes.

questions.q: A program calls fork() 4 times in sequence (no conditions). How many child processes are created?
w: Each fork runs in every existing process.
That's the total number of processes.

questions.q: Which system call can be used by a parent process to determine the termination of child process?
w: wait() blocks until a child terminates and returns its status.

questions.q: A parent process calling _____ system call will be suspended until children processes terminate.
w: The parent sleeps until a child finishes.

questions.q: The exec() family of system calls:
o: Replaces the current process's memory image with a new program

questions.q: The child process can __________
o: be a duplicate of the parent process
never be a duplicate of the parent process
cannot have another program loaded into it
never have another program loaded into it
w: After fork the child is a copy (and it may later exec a new program).

questions.q: The child process completes execution, but the parent keeps executing, then the child process is known as __________
w: Finished child whose exit status hasn't been collected with wait().
questions.h: Zombie = dead child, parent hasn't waited. Orphan = living child, dead parent.

questions.q: A process whose parent has terminated while it is still running is called:
Cascading termination refers to termination of all child processes if the parent process terminates ______
w: Either way, the children are terminated.

questions.q: Cascading termination refers to termination of all child processes if the parent process terminates ______ (options: Normally / Abnormally / Any one / None)
w: Normal or abnormal termination of the parent both trigger it.

questions.q: A process can be terminated due to __________
Restricting the child process to a subset of the parent’s resources prevents any process from __________
o: overloading the system by using a lot of secondary storage
under-loading the system by very less CPU utilization
overloading the system by creating a lot of sub-processes
crashing the system by utilizing multiple resources

questions.q: A single thread of control allows the process to perform __________
o: only one task at a time
only two tasks at a time
w: One thread = one sequence of execution.

questions.q: Which one of the following can not be scheduled by the kernel?
w: Kernel threads are scheduled by the kernel.
The kernel is unaware of user-level threads; the thread library schedules them.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT shared between threads of the same process?
w: Each thread has its own stack (plus registers and PC).
questions.h: Private per thread: ID, PC, registers, stack.

questions.q: Compared with creating a new process, creating a new thread is:
w: No new address space is needed.

questions.q: In the many-to-one threading model, if one user thread makes a blocking system call:
o: The kernel creates a new thread automatically
w: Only one kernel thread serves all user threads.
questions.h: Many-to-one: one block = all block, no parallelism.

questions.q: Linux and Windows mainly use which threading model?
w: Each user thread maps to a kernel thread.

questions.q: What are Multithreaded programs?
o: not at all prone to deadlocks
w: Several threads competing for locks raises deadlock risk.
questions.h: More threads, more locks, more deadlock risk.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of multithreading?
o: Each thread gets a separate address space
Responsiveness — the program can keep responding while one thread is blocked
questions.h: Benefits: Responsiveness, Resource sharing, Economy, Scalability.

questions.q: What is interprocess communication?
o: communication between two threads of same process

questions.q: What is Interprocess communication? (choose the best definition)
o: allows processes to communicate and synchronize their actions when using the same address space
allows processes to communicate and synchronize their actions
allows the processes to only synchronize their actions without communication
w: Processes usually have separate address spaces.

questions.q: Which process can be affected by other processes executing in the system?
w: It shares data with others, so it can affect and be affected.

questions.q: Message passing system allows processes to __________
o: communicate with each other without sharing the same address space
communicate with one another by resorting to shared data
name the recipient or sender of the message
questions.h: Message passing = no shared memory needed.

questions.q: Which IPC model is generally faster for large data exchange after setup?
w: After setup, no kernel involvement per access.
Each message needs a system call.
questions.h: Shared memory = fast; message passing = simpler, works across machines.

questions.q: Which of the following two operations are provided by the IPC facility?
Messages sent by a process __________
o: have to be of a fixed size
have to be a variable size
can be fixed or variable sized
w: Both are supported (trade-off: simple vs flexible).

questions.q: The link between two processes P and Q to send and receive messages is called __________
Which of the following are TRUE for direct communication?
o: A communication link can be associated with N number of process
A communication link is associated with exactly two processes
Exactly N/2 links exist between each pair of processes
Exactly two link exists between each pair of processes

questions.q: In indirect communication between processes P and Q __________
o: there is another process R to handle and pass on the messages between P and Q
there is another machine between the two processes to help communication
there is a mailbox to help communication between P and Q

questions.q: In the non blocking send __________
o: the sending process keeps sending until the message is received
the sending process sends the message and resumes operation
the sending process keeps sending until it receives a message

questions.q: In a blocking (synchronous) receive:
o: The receiver waits until a message is available
The receiver returns immediately with null if no message

questions.q: In the Zero capacity queue __________
o: the queue can store at least one message
the sender blocks until the receiver receives the message
the sender keeps sending and the messages don’t wait in the queue
questions.h: Zero capacity → sender waits for receiver.

questions.q: The Zero Capacity queue __________
o: is referred to as a message system with buffering
is referred to as a message system with no buffering
is referred to as a link

questions.q: Bounded capacity and Unbounded capacity queues are referred to as __________
In a bounded-capacity message queue, if the queue is full the sender:
o: Must block until space is available
questions.h: Bounded full → sender waits. Unbounded → sender never waits.

questions.q: A process that is based on IPC mechanism which executes on different systems and can communicate with other processes using message based communication, is called ________
w: RPC calls a procedure on another machine using messages.
Not the term (Java has RMI = Remote Method Invocation).

questions.q: Which IPC mechanism provides a one-way byte stream between a parent and child process?
w: Created with pipe(); used by related processes.

questions.q: CPU scheduling is the basis of ___________
w: Switching the CPU between processes makes multiprogramming work.

questions.q: In Operating Systems, which of the following is/are CPU scheduling algorithms?
w: All three are CPU scheduling algorithms.
questions.h: FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Priority, RR, MLQ, MLFQ.

questions.q: What are the two steps of a process execution?
w: Execution alternates between CPU and I/O bursts.

questions.q: An I/O bound program will typically have ____________
o: a few very short CPU bursts
a few very short I/O bursts
w: It computes briefly, then waits for I/O again.
questions.h: I/O-bound = many short CPU bursts; CPU-bound = few long ones.

questions.q: A CPU-bound process typically has:
o: A few very long CPU bursts

questions.q: Scheduling is done so as to ____________ (CPU utilization)
w: Keep the CPU as busy as possible.

questions.q: Scheduling is done so as to ____________ (turnaround time)
o: there is no relation between scheduling and turnaround time

questions.q: Scheduling is done so as to __________ (waiting time)
o: keep the waiting time the same
w: Less time in the ready queue.

questions.q: Which scheduling criterion should be MAXIMISED?
w: More processes completed per unit time is better.
questions.h: Maximise CPU utilisation & throughput; minimise the times.

questions.q: The interval from the time of submission of a process to the time of completion is termed as ____________
What is Turnaround time?
o: the total waiting time for a process to finish execution
the total time spent in the ready queue
the total time spent in the running queue
the total time from the completion till the submission of a process
w: i.e. the span between submission and completion.

questions.q: What is Waiting time?
o: the total time in the blocked and waiting queues
the total time spent in the ready queue
the total time spent in the running queue
the total time from the completion till the submission of a process
w: Time waiting for I/O doesn't count.
Waiting time counts only time spent waiting for the CPU.

questions.q: What is Response time?
o: the total time taken from the submission time till the completion time
the total time taken from the submission time till the first response is produced
the total time taken from submission time till the response is output

questions.q: The number of processes completed per unit time is known as __________
12 processes complete in 4 seconds. The throughput is:
In the following cases non – preemptive scheduling occurs?
o: When a process switches from the running state to the ready state
When a process goes from the running state to the waiting state
When a process switches from the waiting state to the ready state
w: It gives up the CPU voluntarily (also on termination).

questions.q: The strategy of making processes that are logically runnable to be temporarily suspended is called ____________
w: A runnable process can be forced off the CPU.

questions.q: Round robin scheduling falls under the category of ____________
w: The timer interrupt takes the CPU away.
questions.h: RR = preemptive FCFS with a quantum.

questions.q: Which algorithm is defined in Time quantum?
w: Each process gets a time quantum.

questions.q: With round robin scheduling algorithm in a time shared system ____________
o: using very large time slices converts it into First come First served scheduling algorithm
using very small time slices converts it into First come First served scheduling algorithm
using extremely small time slices increases performance
using very small time slices converts it into Shortest Job First algorithm
w: Every process finishes within its slice → FCFS.
questions.h: Huge quantum → FCFS; tiny quantum → overhead.

questions.q: There are 10 different processes running on a workstation. Busy processes are scheduled with Round-Robin. Which quantum gives the best response time if processes have short runtimes (less than 10 ms)?
w: Just above the typical burst: most jobs finish in one slice, and others aren't kept waiting long.
Others wait longer for their turn.
questions.h: Quantum slightly larger than a typical burst.

questions.q: Process are classified into different groups in ____________
w: Separate queues for e.g. foreground/background processes.

questions.q: In multilevel feedback scheduling algorithm ____________
o: a process can move to a different classified ready queue
classification of ready queue is permanent
processes are not classified into groups
w: Feedback lets processes move between queues (e.g. by CPU usage or aging).

questions.q: In priority scheduling algorithm ____________
o: CPU is allocated to the process with highest priority
CPU is allocated to the process with lowest priority
Equal priority processes can not be scheduled

questions.q: In priority scheduling algorithm, when a process arrives at the ready queue, its priority is compared with the priority of ____________
w: Only the running one matters for preemption.
If the new one is higher, it preempts (preemptive version).

questions.q: The priority of a process will ______________ if the scheduler assigns it a static priority.
A solution to the problem of indefinite blockage of low – priority processes is ____________
w: Gradually raise the priority of long-waiting processes.

questions.q: A problem encountered in multitasking when a process is perpetually denied necessary resources is called ____________
w: Deadlock is a circular wait among processes.
The process waits indefinitely while others proceed.

questions.q: When high priority task is indirectly preempted by medium priority task effectively inverting the relative priority of the two tasks, the scenario is called __________
w: Low holds a lock the high one needs; medium preempts low.
questions.h: Priority inversion → fix with priority inheritance.

questions.q: Priority inversion is typically solved using:
w: The low-priority lock holder temporarily inherits the high priority.

questions.q: Which of the following statements are true? (I) SRTF may cause starvation (II) Preemptive scheduling may cause starvation (III) Round robin is better than FCFS in terms of response time
w: II and III are also true.
Long jobs can starve under SRTF/preemption; RR gives faster first response.

questions.q: Under multiprogramming, turnaround time for short jobs is usually ________ and that for long jobs is slightly ___________
w: Short jobs no longer wait behind long ones; long jobs share the CPU.
questions.h: Multiprogramming helps short jobs, slightly hurts long ones.

questions.q: The real difficulty with SJF in short term scheduling is ____________
o: it is too good an algorithm
knowing the length of the next CPU request
it is too complex to understand
w: Burst lengths must be predicted (e.g. exponential averaging).
questions.h: SJF problem = predicting the next burst.

questions.q: An SJF algorithm is simply a priority algorithm where the priority is ____________
o: the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst
w: The priority value is the predicted burst: shorter burst → better priority.
Galvin phrases it this way (a larger burst gives a lower priority); the bank key is option A.
It uses the predicted next burst.
questions.h: SJF priority ↔ predicted next CPU burst.
questions.f: Galvin says the priority is "the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst" (a longer burst means lower priority). The bank key is "the predicted next CPU burst". Choose A if this exact question appears.

questions.q: SJF burst prediction using exponential averaging: τₙ₊₁ = α·tₙ + (1 − α)·τₙ. With α = 0.5, last actual burst tₙ = 6 and previous prediction τₙ = 10, the next prediction is:
questions.h: Weighted average of the last actual and last predicted.

questions.q: The FCFS algorithm is particularly troublesome for ____________
w: Galvin: in time-sharing, every user must get the CPU at regular intervals — FCFS can't guarantee this.
This is the bank key, but Galvin's text says time-sharing.
questions.h: FCFS is non-preemptive → bad for interactive time-sharing.
questions.f: The bank key says "multiprogramming systems". Galvin (Operating System Concepts) says "particularly troublesome for time-sharing systems". In the real exam, pick whichever option matches the key, which may be "multiprogramming".

questions.q: The convoy effect is associated with which scheduling algorithm?
w: Short processes wait behind one long CPU-bound process.

questions.q: Which scheduling algorithm allocates the CPU first to the process that requests the CPU first?
What is FIFO algorithm?
o: first executes the job that came in last in the queue
first executes the job that came in first in the queue
first executes the job that needs minimal processor
first executes the job that has maximum processor needs

questions.q: Orders are processed in the sequence they arrive if _______ rule sequences the jobs.
Complex scheduling algorithms ____________
o: are very appropriate for very large computers
w: Large systems can afford the overhead and benefit from it.

questions.q: Consider the following set of processes (burst time in ms): P1 = 6, P2 = 8, P3 = 7, P4 = 3, all arriving at time 0, scheduled with SJF. Which is true?
o: The waiting time for process P1 is 3ms
The waiting time for process P1 is 0ms
The waiting time for process P1 is 16ms
The waiting time for process P1 is 9ms

questions.q: Same processes (P1 = 6, P2 = 8, P3 = 7, P4 = 3, all at 0) under SJF. The average waiting time is:
Same processes (P1 = 6, P2 = 8, P3 = 7, P4 = 3) under FCFS in order P1, P2, P3, P4. Average waiting time?
questions.h: FCFS: each waits for the sum of earlier bursts.

questions.q: P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 arrive at time 0 in that order. FCFS average waiting time is:
w: That's if P2, P3 run first.
questions.h: Long job first = convoy = big average wait.

questions.q: P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 arrive at 0 but run in order P2, P3, P1 (FCFS). Average waiting time?
questions.h: Short jobs first → smaller average wait.

questions.q: P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 arrive at 0 in that order. FCFS average turnaround time is:
Round Robin with quantum 4 ms: P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 (all at 0, order P1, P2, P3). Average waiting time?
questions.h: In RR, wait = completion − arrival − burst.

questions.q: With RR (quantum 4) on P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, when does P2 complete?
w: P2 runs 4-7 and finishes (3 ms needed).

questions.q: SRTF (preemptive SJF): P1 (arrival 0, burst 8), P2 (1, 4), P3 (2, 9), P4 (3, 5). Average waiting time?
questions.h: SRTF: at every arrival, run whoever has the least remaining time.

questions.q: Non-preemptive SJF: P1 (arrival 0, burst 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4). Average waiting time?
questions.h: Non-preemptive: decide only when the CPU becomes free.

questions.q: SRTF on P1 (arrival 0, burst 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4). Average waiting time?
questions.h: Preempt whenever a shorter remaining job arrives.

questions.q: Non-preemptive priority (lower number = higher priority), all arriving at 0: P1 (burst 10, pr 3), P2 (1, pr 1), P3 (2, pr 4), P4 (1, pr 5), P5 (5, pr 2). Average waiting time?
questions.h: Sort by priority number, then compute waits.

questions.q: Which algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes (all available at time 0)?
w: Provably optimal for average waiting time.
Good response, not minimum average wait.

questions.q: When several processes access the same data concurrently and the outcome of the execution depends on the particular order in which the access takes place is called ________
w: The result depends on who "wins the race".

questions.q: If a process is executing in its critical section, then no other processes can be executing in their critical section. What is this condition called?
questions.h: One in the CS at a time = mutual exclusion.

questions.q: Mutual exclusion implies that ____________
o: if a process is executing in its critical section, then no other process must be executing in their critical sections
if a process is executing in its critical section, then other processes must be executing in their critical sections
if a process is executing in its critical section, then all the resources of the system must be blocked until it finishes execution

questions.q: Bounded waiting implies that there exists a bound on the number of times a process is allowed to enter its critical section ____________
o: after a process has made a request to enter its critical section and before the request is granted
when another process is in its critical section
before a process has made a request to enter its critical section
w: No process waits forever while others keep entering.

questions.q: The "progress" requirement of a critical-section solution says:
o: Every process must enter its CS in strict turns
If no process is in its CS, the selection of the next one to enter cannot be postponed indefinitely, and only processes wanting to enter take part
A process must leave its CS within a time limit
questions.h: Progress = no needless blocking when the CS is free.

questions.q: A minimum of _____ variable(s) is/are required to be shared between processes to solve the critical section problem.
w: A single turn variable forces strict alternation (no progress).
Peterson's solution uses flag[] and turn.

questions.q: Peterson's solution for two processes uses which shared variables?
w: flag shows intent, turn breaks ties.

o: It does not ensure mutual exclusion
It does not ensure bounded waiting
It requires that processes enter the critical section in strict alternation
It does not prevent deadlocks but ensures mutual exclusion
w: A process enters only if the other's flag is false after setting its own.
If both set their flags at the same time, both spin forever.
questions.h: Flags only (no turn) → mutual exclusion ✓, deadlock possible ✗.

w: They must take strict turns, so one can block the other from re-entering even when the CS is free.
This is the bank key, but strict alternation violates progress.
questions.f: Correction: the bank key says "Both mutual exclusion and progress". This is GATE CS 2010, whose official answer is "Mutual exclusion but not progress", because the code forces strict alternation.

questions.q: Semaphore is a/an _______ to solve the critical section problem.
w: A semaphore is an integer variable accessed atomically (through wait and signal).
questions.f: This question is garbled in the bank. The usual version reads "Semaphore is a/an ___" with the answer "integer variable". Here, pick "atomically".

questions.q: What are the two atomic operations permissible on semaphores?
A semaphore is a shared integer variable __________
o: that can not drop below zero
that can not be more than zero
that can not drop below one
that can not be more than one
w: In the classical (busy-wait) definition, wait() blocks at 0, so it never goes negative.
Only binary semaphores are limited to 1.

questions.q: Which one of the following is a synchronization tool?
w: Used for mutual exclusion and ordering.

questions.q: Mutual exclusion can be provided by the __________
o: both mutex locks and binary semaphores
w: Both allow one holder at a time.

questions.q: Process synchronization can be done on __________
A counting semaphore S is initialised to 10. Then 6 P (wait) operations and 4 V (signal) operations are performed. The final value of S is:
A counting semaphore is initialised to 7. After 20 P operations and 15 V operations, its value is:
All processes share a semaphore mutex initialised to 1. A process executes signal(mutex); … critical section … wait(mutex). In this situation:
o: processes will starve to enter critical section
several processes maybe executing in their critical section
w: The opposite — too many get in.
The initial signal raises mutex to 2, so mutual exclusion is broken.

questions.q: All processes share a semaphore mutex initialised to 1. A process executes wait(mutex); … critical section … wait(mutex). In this situation:
o: processes will starve to enter critical section
several processes maybe executing in their critical section
w: The second wait blocks forever (mutex is 0 and never signalled).
P0 prints once; P1 and P2 each release S0. If those releases are separate, P0 prints 3 times; if they overlap on a binary semaphore, only twice.
P1/P2 release S0 at least once more.
questions.h: Binary semaphore releases can "merge" → 2 or 3 → at least twice.

questions.q: Each process Pi, i = 0…9, runs: repeat P(mutex); {CS}; V(mutex) forever. P10 is identical but uses V(mutex) instead of P(mutex). With mutex initialised to 1, what is the largest number of processes that can be inside the CS at any moment?
w: P10's extra V lets more in.
The standard answer to this GATE question is 3.
questions.f: This is GATE 1997. The accepted answer is 3, as the bank says.

questions.q: Process A: A1: Y = X*2; A2: X = Y. Process B: B1: Z = X+1; B2: X = Z. X = 5 initially; statements of A and B can interleave in any order. How many different final values of X are possible?
w: Only the two sequential orders give 11 and 12.
Possible results: 11 (A then B), 12 (B then A), 10 and 6 (interleaved, one update lost).

questions.q: Same processes, but now B does wait(T) before B1 and A does signal(T) after A2 (T = 0, X = 5). How many different final values of X are possible?
w: B can start only after A finishes: X = 10, then 11. Only one outcome.
questions.h: Semaphore forces an order → one result.

questions.q: A monitor is a module that encapsulates __________
o: procedures that operate on shared data structure
w: A monitor bundles data, procedures and synchronisation.

questions.q: To enable a process to wait within the monitor __________
o: a condition variable must be declared as condition
condition variables must be used as boolean objects
w: e.g. condition x; then x.wait() / x.signal().
questions.h: Wait inside a monitor → condition variable.

questions.q: In the bounded-buffer producer–consumer problem with semaphores, typical initial values are:
w: Buffer starts empty with n free slots.
Buffer isn't full at the start.

questions.q: The dining philosophers problem illustrates:
o: Deadlock and starvation in resource allocation
w: Each philosopher needs two shared forks.

questions.q: Test-and-Set is an example of:
o: A hardware atomic instruction for synchronisation
w: Reads and sets a lock in one indivisible step.

questions.q: A set of processes is deadlock if __________
o: each process is blocked and will remain so forever
all processes are trying to kill each other
w: Every process waits on another in the set.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
w: It's NO preemption that is required.
questions.h: ME, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait.

questions.q: For Mutual exclusion to prevail in the system ____________
o: at least one resource must be held in a non sharable mode
the processor must be a uniprocessor rather than a multiprocessor
there must be at least one resource in a sharable mode

questions.q: For a Hold and wait condition to prevail ____________
o: A process must not be holding a resource, but waiting for one to be freed
A process must be holding at least one resource and waiting to acquire additional resources that are being held by other processes
A process must hold at least one resource and not be waiting to acquire additional resources

questions.q: For sharable resources, mutual exclusion ____________
o: may be or may not be required
w: Sharable resources can be used together.
e.g. read-only files can be shared freely.
questions.h: Sharable → no mutual exclusion → can't deadlock on it.

questions.q: Deadlock prevention is a set of methods ___________
o: to ensure that at least one of the necessary conditions cannot hold
to ensure that all of the necessary conditions do not hold
to decide if the requested resources for a process have to be given or not
w: Breaking any one condition prevents deadlock.

questions.q: The circular wait condition can be prevented by ____________
o: defining a linear ordering of resource types
w: Request resources only in increasing order → no cycle.

questions.q: The disadvantage of a process being allocated all its resources before beginning its execution is ____________
w: Resources sit idle while held but not yet used (also starvation).

questions.q: To ensure no preemption, if a process is holding some resources and requests another resource that cannot be immediately allocated to it ____________
o: then the process waits for the resources be allocated to it
the process keeps sending requests until the resource is allocated to it
the process resumes execution without the resource being allocated to it
then all resources currently being held are preempted
w: They are released and requested again later — this breaks "no preemption".
questions.h: Can't get more? Give up all you hold.

questions.q: To avoid deadlock ____________
o: there must be a fixed number of resources to allocate
resource allocation must be done only once
all deadlocked processes must be aborted
w: The bank's answer — avoidance needs known, fixed resources.
questions.h: Avoidance: fixed resources + known maximum needs.

questions.q: The request and release of resources are ___________
What is a reusable resource?
o: that can be used by one process at a time and is not depleted by that use
that can be used by more than one process at a time
that can be shared between various threads
questions.h: Reusable = one at a time, not used up.

questions.q: Given a priori information about the ________ number of resources of each type that maybe requested for each process, it is possible to construct an algorithm that ensures that the system will never enter a deadlock state.
w: Avoidance (Banker's) needs each process's maximum claim.

questions.q: A deadlock avoidance algorithm dynamically examines the __________ to ensure that a circular wait condition can never exist.
Each request requires that the system consider the _____________ to decide whether the current request can be satisfied or must wait to avoid a future possible deadlock.
o: processes that have previously been in the system
resources currently allocated to each process
future requests and releases of each process
w: Also considered (Galvin), but not the bank key.
Also considered (Galvin), but not the bank key.
questions.f: Galvin lists three things: resources currently available, resources currently allocated to each process, and future requests and releases. The bank key is "resources currently available".

questions.q: A system is in the safe state if ____________
o: the system can allocate resources to each process in some order and still avoid a deadlock
w: Galvin's definition of a safe state.
Also true (it's equivalent), but the bank key is the first option.
The bank key is the first option.
questions.h: Safe = some order exists that avoids deadlock.
questions.f: "There exists a safe sequence" is equivalent and also true. The bank key is option A.

questions.q: A system is in a safe state only if there exists a ____________
w: An order in which every process can finish.

questions.q: Which statement about safe and unsafe states is TRUE?
o: An unsafe state is always a deadlock
A safe state guarantees no deadlock; an unsafe state may lead to deadlock
w: Unsafe may lead to deadlock, but isn't necessarily one.
Deadlocked states are a subset of unsafe states.
It refuses requests that lead to them.

questions.q: A system has 12 magnetic tape drives and 3 processes. Max needs: P0 = 10, P1 = 4, P2 = 9. Currently allocated: P0 = 5, P1 = 2, P2 = 2. Which of the following sequence is a safe sequence?
w: Available is 3; P0 needs 5 — can't go first.
After P1, available = 5; P2 needs 7 — can't.
questions.h: Available = total − allocated = 12 − 9 = 3. Need = Max − Alloc.

questions.q: Same system (12 drives; P0 max 10, alloc 5; P1 max 4, alloc 2; P2 max 9, alloc 2). If P2 requests and is given 1 more drive, the state becomes:
w: Available drops to 2: only P1 can finish (→ 4), then P0 needs 5 and P2 needs 6 — neither can finish.
The request can physically be granted.
questions.h: Galvin's classic: granting P2 one more drive → unsafe.

w: Safe sequence e.g. P1, P3, P4, P2, P0.
questions.h: Need = Max − Alloc → P1 (1,2,2) fits Available first.

questions.q: In the same Banker's example, what is the Need of P0?
In the same Banker's example, which process can be satisfied FIRST with Available (3,3,2)?
questions.h: Pick any process with Need ≤ Available.

questions.q: The Banker’s algorithm is _____________ than the resource allocation graph algorithm.
w: It handles multiple instances but costs more (O(m·n²)).
The RAG algorithm is cheaper (single instance only).

questions.q: The resource allocation graph is not applicable to a resource allocation system ____________
o: with multiple instances of each resource type
with a single instance of each resource type
single & multiple instances of each resource type
w: The RAG algorithm only works for single-instance resources.

questions.q: The wait-for graph is a deadlock detection algorithm that is applicable when ____________
o: all resources have a single instance
all resources have multiple instances (repeated option)
w: Collapse the RAG into process-to-process edges.

questions.q: An edge from process Pi to Pj in a wait for graph indicates that ____________
o: Pi is waiting for Pj to release a resource that Pi needs
Pj is waiting for Pi to release a resource that Pj needs
w: Pi → Pj = Pi waits on Pj.
questions.h: Arrow points to the one you wait for.

questions.q: If the wait for graph contains a cycle ____________
o: then a deadlock does not exist
either deadlock exists or system is in a safe state
w: For single-instance resources, a cycle ⇔ deadlock.

questions.q: In a resource allocation graph with MULTIPLE instances per resource, a cycle means:
o: A deadlock may or may not exist
w: Another instance may free up and break the cycle.

questions.q: If deadlocks occur frequently, the detection algorithm must be invoked ________
w: Catch them early before many processes get stuck.

questions.q: For an effective operating system, when to check for deadlock?
o: every time a resource request is made
every time a resource request is made at fixed time intervals
questions.h: Bank answer: on requests, at fixed intervals.

questions.q: Three processes each need at most 2 units of a resource. What is the minimum number of units that guarantees no deadlock?
A system has 6 identical resources and n processes, each needing at most 3. What is the maximum n that guarantees deadlock freedom?
Recovery from deadlock can be done by:
w: That's the ostrich approach, not recovery.

questions.q: The operating system and the other processes are protected from being modified by an already running process because ____________
o: every address generated by the CPU is being checked against the relocation and limit registers
they are in different memory spaces
they are in different logical addresses
w: The check is what enforces it.
questions.h: Base + limit check on every address.

questions.q: With base (relocation) register 14000 and limit 3000, logical address 2500 maps to:
With base 14000 and limit 3000, logical address 3200 results in:
The operating system maintains a ______ table that keeps track of how many frames have been allocated, how many are there, and how many are available.
w: The page table maps one process's pages.
The frame table tracks every physical frame.

questions.q: To obtain better memory utilization, dynamic loading is used. With dynamic loading, a routine is not loaded until it is called. For implementing dynamic loading ____________
o: special support from operating system is essential
special support from hardware is required
user programs can implement dynamic loading without any special support from hardware or operating system
special support from both hardware and operating system is essential
questions.h: Dynamic loading = user-level. Dynamic linking = OS help.

questions.q: Swapping _______ be done when a process has pending I/O, or has to execute I/O operations only into operating system buffers.
w: The I/O could write into memory now used by another process.

questions.q: Memory holes of 100K, 500K, 200K, 300K, 600K (in order). Using FIRST fit, where does a 212K process go?
w: First hole that is large enough.

questions.q: Holes: 100K, 500K, 200K, 300K, 600K. Using BEST fit, the 212K process goes into:
Holes 100K, 500K, 200K, 300K, 600K; processes 212K, 417K, 112K, 426K arrive in order. Which strategy places ALL four?
questions.h: Galvin example: only best fit places all four.

questions.q: Total free memory is enough for a request but it is scattered in small non-contiguous holes. This is:
w: Fixed by compaction or by paging.
That is unused space inside allocated blocks.

questions.q: Paging eliminates which type of fragmentation?
w: Paging still has internal fragmentation (last page).
Any free frame can be used.

questions.q: A process of 72,766 bytes uses 2,048-byte pages. Internal fragmentation is:
w: That's the used part of the last page.
questions.h: Waste = pages × page size − process size.

questions.q: A logical address space is 32 bits with 4 KB pages and 4-byte page table entries. The page table size is:
Physical memory 64 MB and frame size 4 KB. Number of frames is:
With a 1 KB page size, logical address 3085 refers to page ___ offset ___:
questions.h: page = addr div size, offset = addr mod size.

questions.q: Segmentation divides a program into:
o: Variable-size logical units such as code, data and stack

questions.q: The _________ presents a uniform device-access interface to the I/O subsystem, much as system calls provide a standard interface between the application and the operating system.
w: They hide device-specific details from the kernel.

questions.q: In a memory mapped input/output __________
o: the CPU uses polling to watch the control bit constantly, looping to see if a device is ready
the CPU writes one data byte to the data register and sets a bit in control register to show that a byte is available
the CPU receives an interrupt when the device is ready for the next byte
the CPU runs a user written code and does accordingly
w: Device registers are accessed like memory locations.
questions.h: Memory-mapped I/O: device registers = memory addresses.

questions.q: If the sum of the working set sizes increases, exceeding the total number of available frames ____________
o: the operating system selects a process to suspend
w: Swapping one out frees frames and prevents thrashing.
questions.h: Too much demand → suspend a process.

questions.q: Thrashing occurs when:
o: The CPU is idle because there are no processes
Processes spend more time paging than executing
w: Too few frames → constant page faults.

questions.q: As the degree of multiprogramming increases beyond a point, CPU utilisation drops sharply. This is due to:
w: Each process gets too few frames.

questions.q: Belady's anomaly is that, for some reference strings:
o: Increasing the number of frames increases page faults (FIFO)
LRU gives more faults than FIFO
questions.h: Belady = FIFO + more frames → more faults.

questions.q: Which page replacement algorithm suffers from Belady's anomaly?
Reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 1 2 0 1 7 0 1, 3 frames, FIFO. Number of page faults?
Same string (7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 1 2 0 1 7 0 1), 3 frames, LRU. Page faults?
Same string, 3 frames, Optimal (OPT). Page faults?
w: Too few (6 distinct pages give at least 6 faults, but the true answer is 9).

questions.q: Reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 with FIFO and 3 frames gives how many faults?
Reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, FIFO with 4 frames gives:
w: More frames, more faults — Belady's anomaly.

questions.q: Reference string 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2 with 3 frames and LRU. Number of page faults?
questions.h: LRU evicts the page used longest ago.

questions.q: The page replacement algorithm that gives the lowest possible page-fault rate is:
o: Optimal (replace the page not used for the longest future time)
w: Needs future knowledge — used as a benchmark.
questions.h: OPT = best but impossible in practice.

questions.q: Memory access 200 ns, page-fault service 8 ms, page-fault rate 1 in 1000. Effective access time is about:
Demand paging means:
o: A page is brought into memory only when it is referenced
All pages are loaded at start
Pages are loaded in advance by prediction only

questions.q: Copy-on-write is used to make which system call efficient?
w: Parent and child share pages until one of them writes.

questions.q: The information about all files is kept in ____________
w: The directory (on disk) holds the entries for all files.

questions.q: The operating system keeps a small table containing information about all open files called ____________
w: Speeds up access to open files.

questions.q: What will happen in the single level directory?
o: All files are contained in the same directory
All files are contained in different directories all at the same level

questions.q: The main problem of a single-level directory is:
o: Naming collisions and no grouping — all users share one namespace
w: Every file needs a unique name.

questions.q: The operating system _______ the links when traversing directory trees, to preserve the acyclic structure of the system.
Which file allocation method suffers from external fragmentation?
w: Files need runs of free blocks.
Any free block can be used.
Any free block can be used.

questions.q: Which allocation method does NOT support efficient direct (random) access?
w: You must follow pointers from the start.
The index block gives direct pointers.

questions.q: Unix inodes are an example of:
o: Indexed allocation (with direct and indirect pointers)

questions.q: Disk queue 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 with the head at 53. Total head movement with FCFS is:
questions.h: FCFS: sum of jumps in arrival order.

questions.q: Same queue (98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67; head 53) with SSTF. Total head movement?
questions.h: SSTF: always go to the nearest request.

questions.q: Which disk scheduling algorithm can cause starvation of far-away requests?
w: Nearby requests keep getting served first.

questions.q: The SCAN disk scheduling algorithm is also known as:
w: The head sweeps back and forth like a lift.

questions.q: Disk access time consists of:
o: Seek time + rotational latency + transfer time
w: Move the arm, wait for the sector, read it.
